docs.text:
• Wooldridge: Chapter 2, Section 2.3 (Properties of OLS on any sample), particularly the derivation of SST = SSE + SSR and the definition of \(R^2\)
  • R: After fit <- lm(y ~ x), use anova(fit) to see SSR (residual SS) and SSE (model SS) directly; sum(resid(fit)) verifies Property 1
  • Python: results = ols(...).fit() → results.ssr (SSR), results.ess (SSE), results.centered_tss (SST)

docs.title: Lesson M02.L04: Units, Functional Forms, and R-Squared
docs.text: Field Detail Module M02 — Simple Linear Regression (Wooldridge Chapter 2) Level Graduate Duration 35 minutes Learning Objective Interpret \(R^2\) correctly; predict how coefficient estimates change under rescaling; choose and interpret log-linear and log-log functional forms. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 7th ed., Chapter 2, Sections 2.4 (units and functional form) and 2.3 (\(R^2\))

docs.title: 1. R-Squared: Definition and Interpretation
docs.text:
From M02.L03, we established the decomposition \(SST = SSE + SSR\). This motivates:

\[R^2 = \frac{SSE}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSR}{SST}\]

Interpretation: \(R^2\) is the fraction of total sample variation in \(y\) that is explained (linearly) by \(x\).

Key properties:

Fact Explanation \(R^2 \in [0, 1]\) SSE and SSR are non-negative and sum to SST \(R^2 = 0\) \(x\) explains none of the variation in \(y\); \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0\) and \(\hat{y}_i = \bar{y}\) for all \(i\) \(R^2 = 1\) Perfect fit: every observation lies on the regression line; \(\hat{u}_i = 0\) for all \(i\) \(R^2 = r_{xy}^2\) In simple regression, \(R^2\) equals the square of the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\)

docs.title: 2. Effect of Changing Units on OLS Estimates
docs.text: A critical skill: knowing how \(\hat{\beta}_0\), \(\hat{\beta}_1\), and \(R^2\) respond when you rescale variables.

docs.title: Case A: Multiply the dependent variable \(y\) by a constant \(c\)
docs.text:
Define \(y^* = c \cdot y\). Running OLS of \(y^*\) on \(x\):

\[\hat{\beta}_1^* = c \cdot \hat{\beta}_1, \qquad \hat{\beta}_0^* = c \cdot \hat{\beta}_0, \qquad R^2 \text{ unchanged}\]

Intuition: Every \(y_i\) is scaled by \(c\), so every \(\hat{y}_i\) must also scale by \(c\) to minimise the new SSR. Both SSE and SST scale by \(c^2\), so their ratio \(R^2\) is unchanged.

Example: If wages are in dollars and you convert to cents (\(c = 100\)), the slope multiplies by 100 (dollars-per-year becomes cents-per-year), but \(R^2\) stays the same.

docs.title: Case B: Multiply the independent variable \(x\) by a constant \(c\)
docs.text:
Define \(x^* = c \cdot x\). Running OLS of \(y\) on \(x^*\):

\[\hat{\beta}_1^* = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1}{c}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_0^* = \hat{\beta}_0, \qquad R^2 \text{ unchanged}\]

Intuition: A one-unit change in \(x^*\) corresponds to a \(c\)-unit change in the original \(x\). So the slope (effect per unit of regressor) must be divided by \(c\) to keep predicted values identical. The intercept (value when \(x^* = 0\), i.e. \(x = 0\)) is unchanged.

Example: If education is measured in months instead of years (\(c = 12\)), the slope divides by 12, but \(R^2\) and \(\hat{\beta}_0\) are unchanged.

Summary table:

Change \(\hat{\beta}_1\) \(\hat{\beta}_0\) \(R^2\) \(y \to c \cdot y\) \(\times c\) \(\times c\) unchanged \(x \to c \cdot x\) \(\div c\) unchanged unchanged \(y \to c \cdot y\) and \(x \to d \cdot x\) \(\times (c/d)\) \(\times c\) unchanged

docs.title: 3. Functional Forms: Why Log Transformations?
docs.text:
The linear model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\) assumes a constant additive effect: one unit of \(x\) always changes \(y\) by \(\beta_1\), regardless of the level of \(x\). For many economic variables, this is unrealistic.

Common reasons to use \(\log(y)\) or \(\log(x)\):

  1. Right-skewed distributions: Wages, income, prices, and GDP are typically right-skewed with a few very large values. \(\log(\text{wage})\) is much more symmetric and closer to normally distributed.
  2. Elasticity interpretation: Taking logs converts the slope into a percentage-change interpretation — often more natural in economics.
  3. Heteroskedasticity reduction: Log transforms often stabilise variance across the range of \(x\) (relevant for inference; covered in later modules).

Note: \(\log\) in econometrics almost always means the natural logarithm (base \(e\), denoted \(\ln\) in mathematics). Wooldridge writes \(\log\) throughout and means \(\ln\).

docs.title: 4. The Log-Linear Model (Semi-Elasticity)
docs.text:
Model:

\[\log(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\]

Interpretation of \(\hat{\beta}_1\):

Using the approximation \(\Delta \log(y) \approx \Delta y / y\) (valid for small changes):

\[\hat{\beta}_1 \approx \frac{\% \Delta y}{100 \cdot \Delta x}\]

More precisely: a one-unit increase in \(x\) is associated with approximately a \(100 \cdot \hat{\beta}_1\)% change in \(y\).

This is called a semi-elasticity — the dependent variable is in logs but the independent variable is in levels.

Example: If \(\log(\text{wage}) = 1.2 + 0.08 \times \text{Educ} + u\): → One additional year of education is associated with approximately an 8% increase in wages. → More precisely: the multiplicative factor is \(e^{0.08} \approx 1.0833\), so wages increase by about 8.33%.

docs.title: 5. The Log-Log Model (Constant Elasticity)
docs.text:
Model:

\[\log(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(x) + u\]

Interpretation of \(\hat{\beta}_1\):

\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\% \Delta y}{\% \Delta x} \quad \text{(elasticity)}\]

A 1% increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(\hat{\beta}_1\)% change in \(y\). The slope is a constant elasticity.

Example: If \(\log(\text{sales}) = 2.0 - 0.5 \times \log(\text{price}) + u\): → A 1% increase in price is associated with a 0.5% decrease in sales. → \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.5\) is the price elasticity of demand (inelastic demand).

docs.title: 6. When to Use Each Form
docs.text:
Model \(x\) \(y\) Slope Interpretation Level-Level levels levels \(\Delta y\) per 1-unit \(\Delta x\) Log-Level (semi-elasticity) levels logs \(\approx \%\Delta y\) per 1-unit \(\Delta x\) Level-Log logs levels \(\Delta y\) per 1% \(\Delta x\) Log-Log (elasticity) logs logs \(\%\Delta y\) per 1% \(\Delta x\)

Rule of thumb: Take the log of a variable if: - It has a strongly right-skewed distribution (positive values only, large range) - You want to interpret the coefficient as a percentage or elasticity - The relationship between \(y\) and \(x\) appears curved (concave) rather than linear

docs.title: 7. A Note on R-Squared Across Models
docs.text:
You cannot compare \(R^2\) across models with different dependent variables.

A log-wage regression (\(\log(\text{wage})\) as \(y\)) and a wage-level regression (\(\text{wage}\) as \(y\)) have different SSTs and are not comparable by \(R^2\).

Is a low R² bad? Not necessarily. \(R^2\) measures how much variation in \(y\) is explained by a single regressor. In cross-sectional economic data:

  • A regression of wages on education alone with \(R^2 = 0.15\) is typical and informative
  • The low \(R^2\) reflects that wages depend on many factors (ability, experience, employer, location) — not that the education coefficient is wrong or unimportant
  • If \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is statistically significant (tested in Module 4) and economically meaningful in magnitude, the regression adds real value regardless of \(R^2\)

Key principle: \(R^2\) measures fit, not the validity, significance, or economic importance of a regression coefficient. Researchers who chase high \(R^2\) by adding irrelevant variables are making a mistake (the adjusted-\(R^2\) problem is addressed in later modules on multiple regression).

docs.title: Setting: Log-Wage Regression
docs.text:
A researcher estimates the following log-linear model on \(n = 526\) workers from the CPS wage dataset (from Wooldridge, Chapter 2):

\[\widehat{\log(\text{wage})} = 0.584 + 0.083 \times \text{Educ}\]

with \(R^2 = 0.186\).

Interpretation of the slope:

\(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.083\): Each additional year of education is associated with approximately a 8.3% increase in hourly wage.

(More precisely: \(e^{0.083} - 1 = 0.0865\), so about 8.65% — the approximation \(\approx 8.3\%\) is good for small values.)

Interpretation of the intercept:

\(\hat{\beta}_0 = 0.584\): A worker with zero years of education is predicted to have \(\log(\text{wage}) = 0.584\), corresponding to \(\text{wage} = e^{0.584} \approx \$1.79\)/hour. Again, this is extrapolation far outside the data range (minimum education in the sample is typically 0–1 years) and should not be taken literally.

Predicted wage for a college graduate (16 years of education):

\[\widehat{\log(\text{wage})} = 0.584 + 0.083 \times 16 = 0.584 + 1.328 = 1.912\] \[\widehat{\text{wage}} = e^{1.912} \approx \$6.77 \text{ per hour}\]

(Note: this dataset is from the early 1990s — the wage level reflects that era.)

Interpretation of \(R^2 = 0.186\):

Education alone explains approximately 18.6% of the variation in log wages. The remaining 81.4% reflects other factors (experience, industry, location, ability, etc.). This is a typical result for a single-variable wage regression and does not indicate a flawed model.

Effect of a units change: Suppose wages are measured in cents rather than dollars (\(y^* = 100 \times \text{wage}\)). Since we're working with \(\log(y^*)\):

\[\log(y^*) = \log(100 \times \text{wage}) = \log(100) + \log(\text{wage}) = 4.605 + \log(\text{wage})\]

So \(\hat{\beta}_0^* = 0.584 + 4.605 = 5.189\), while \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.083\) is unchanged (the log transform absorbs the scale change into the intercept), and \(R^2\) is unchanged.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"A low R² means the regression is useless."

This is one of the most persistent misconceptions in applied econometrics.

\(R^2\) measures goodness of fit — how much of the variation in \(y\) the model explains. But the research question is often not "how much of \(y\) do I explain?" but rather "what is the effect of \(x\) on \(y\)?"

Consider this thought experiment: Suppose we regress individual annual income on whether the person was born in January vs. all other months. The \(R^2\) will be tiny — month of birth explains almost none of income variation. But in a randomised experiment, even a tiny \(R^2\) provides an unbiased estimate of the treatment effect; the regression is perfectly valid.

The relevant criteria for a useful regression are:

  1. Is \(\hat{\beta}_1\) statistically significantly different from zero? (Hypothesis testing, Module 4)
  2. Is the magnitude of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) economically meaningful?
  3. Are the assumptions (especially SLR.4: \(E(u|x) = 0\)) plausibly satisfied?

\(R^2\) answers none of these questions. Maximising \(R^2\) by adding variables indiscriminately can actually harm inference (see adjusted-\(R^2\) and overfitting in Module 3).

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
A regression of housing price (in $'000s) on house size (in square feet) yields:

\[\widehat{\text{Price}} = 40.0 + 0.12 \times \text{Size}, \qquad R^2 = 0.62\]

(a) Interpret \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.12\) in context. (b) If prices are instead measured in dollars (not $'000s), what is the new \(\hat{\beta}_1^*\)? (c) If size is instead measured in hundreds of square feet, what is the new \(\hat{\beta}_1^*\)? (d) In both (b) and (c), what happens to \(R^2\)?

Show Answer

(a) Each additional square foot of house size is associated with, on average, $120 more in house price (since price is in $'000s, so 0.12 × $1000 = $120 per sq ft).

(b) Converting price to dollars multiplies \(y\) by 1000 (\(c = 1000\)): \(\hat{\beta}_1^* = 0.12 \times 1000 = 120\) (dollars per square foot). \(\hat{\beta}_0^* = 40.0 \times 1000 = 40{,}000\) dollars.

(c) Converting size to hundreds of sq ft multiplies \(x\) by \(c = 100\): \(\hat{\beta}_1^* = 0.12 / 100 \times 100 = 0.12 \times 100 / 100\)... more carefully: if \(x^* = x/100\) (size in hundreds), we're dividing \(x\) by 100, i.e. \(c = 1/100\), so \(\hat{\beta}_1^* = 0.12 \div (1/100) = 12\). Interpretation: each additional 100 sq ft is associated with $12,000 more in price (since price is still in $'000s: \(12 \times \$1000 = \$12{,}000\)). \(\hat{\beta}_0\) unchanged at 40.0.

(d) \(R^2 = 0.62\) in all cases. \(R^2\) is invariant to linear rescaling of \(x\) or \(y\).

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
A researcher estimates two models on wages:

  • Model A (level-level): \(\widehat{\text{Wage}} = -4.20 + 1.35 \times \text{Educ}\), \(R^2 = 0.974\)
  • Model B (log-level): \(\widehat{\log(\text{Wage})} = 1.05 + 0.09 \times \text{Educ}\), \(R^2 = 0.961\)

(a) Interpret \(\hat{\beta}_1\) in Model A and Model B. (b) Can you conclude Model A is better than Model B because its \(R^2\) is higher? (c) What predicted wage does each model give for \(\text{Educ} = 14\)?

Show Answer

(a) Model A: Each additional year of education is associated with $1.35/hour more in wages (level effect). Model B: Each additional year of education is associated with approximately 9% more in wages (semi-elasticity). Model B is usually preferred for wages because it respects the lower bound of zero (log-wage can be any real number; predicted wage is always positive) and captures the multiplicative nature of wage growth.

(b) No. The \(R^2\) values come from regressions with different dependent variables (Wage vs. \(\log(\text{Wage})\)). SST for wages (\(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2\)) is completely different from SST for log-wages. The \(R^2\) values are not comparable. Model selection between these functional forms should be based on economic theory, distributional assumptions, and specification tests — not \(R^2\) comparison.

(c) Model A: \(\widehat{\text{Wage}} = -4.20 + 1.35 \times 14 = -4.20 + 18.90 = \$14.70\)/hr. Model B: \(\widehat{\log(\text{Wage})} = 1.05 + 0.09 \times 14 = 1.05 + 1.26 = 2.31\); \(\widehat{\text{Wage}} = e^{2.31} \approx \$10.07\)/hr.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
A log-log model is estimated for coffee sales:

\[\widehat{\log(\text{Cups})} = 8.5 - 1.2 \times \log(\text{Price})\]

(a) Interpret \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.2\). (b) Is demand for coffee elastic or inelastic with respect to price? (c) If price rises by 10%, what is the predicted percentage change in cups sold? (d) A competitor's model uses levels: \(\widehat{\text{Cups}} = 5000 - 800 \times \text{Price}\). Can you compare the two models' \(R^2\) values? Why or why not?

Show Answer

(a) \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.2\) is the price elasticity of demand: a 1% increase in price is associated with a 1.2% decrease in cups sold.

(b) Since \(|\hat{\beta}_1| = 1.2 > 1\), demand is elastic with respect to price — consumers are relatively price-sensitive for coffee in this sample.

(c) A 10% price increase → predicted change in cups = \(-1.2 \times 10\% = -12\%\).

(d) No. The dependent variable in the log-log model is \(\log(\text{Cups})\) while the level model uses \(\text{Cups}\). These have different SSTs and the \(R^2\) values are not comparable. To compare models with different functional forms for \(y\), researchers typically use information criteria (AIC, BIC) or correlation-based measures that account for the transformation.

docs.title: 1. From Algebra to Statistics
docs.text:
Lessons M02.L02–L04 established algebraic properties of OLS — things that are true by definition, in every sample, regardless of how the data were generated.

Now we shift to statistical properties: what can we say about OLS estimators across repeated samples drawn from the same population? For this, we need to specify how the data were generated — i.e., we need assumptions about the data generating process (DGP).

docs.title: SLR.1 — Linear in Parameters
docs.text:
Assumption: The population model is:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\]

where \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are the unknown population parameters we want to estimate.

Key clarification: "Linear in parameters" does NOT mean the relationship between \(y\) and \(x\) must be linear. For example:

\[\log(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(x) + u\]

is linear in the parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) even though it implies a nonlinear (log-log) relationship between \(y\) and \(x\). SLR.1 is satisfied.

What would violate SLR.1? A model like \(y = \beta_0 \cdot e^{\beta_1 x} + u\) — here \(\beta_1\) enters nonlinearly and OLS cannot be directly applied.

docs.title: SLR.2 — Random Sampling
docs.text:
Assumption: \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) is a random sample of size \(n\) drawn from the population model.

Implication: Each observation is independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from the same joint distribution of \((x, y)\). No observation is special or selected based on the outcome.

Common violations: Time-series data (observations are correlated over time); panel data (same person observed repeatedly); choice-based sampling (e.g. only surveying employed workers when studying wages).

docs.title: SLR.3 — Sample Variation in x (No Perfect Collinearity)
docs.text:
Assumption: In the sample, \(x\) is not constant:

\[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 > 0\]

Why it's needed: The OLS slope formula \(\hat{\beta}_1 = \sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y}) / \sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2\) requires a non-zero denominator. If all \(x_i\) are identical, we cannot estimate the effect of changing \(x\) — there's no variation to learn from.

Common violation: Multicollinearity (near-perfect collinearity among regressors in multiple regression; simple regression only has one \(x\) so exact collinearity is obvious).

docs.title: SLR.4 — Zero Conditional Mean Error
docs.text:
Assumption: The expected value of the error, conditional on \(x\), is zero:

\[E(u \mid x) = 0\]

This is the crucial assumption. It means that, for any given value of \(x\), the unobservable factors in \(u\) are on average zero. Equivalently, \(u\) and \(x\) are mean-independent — knowing \(x\) tells you nothing about the average of \(u\).

Implications of SLR.4:

  • \(E(u) = 0\) (unconditionally)
  • \(\text{Cov}(x, u) = 0\) (zero covariance between \(x\) and \(u\))
  • \(E(y \mid x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) (the population regression function is the conditional expectation of \(y\) given \(x\))

What violates SLR.4?

Violation Explanation Omitted Variable Bias (OVB) If a variable \(z\) affects \(y\) and is correlated with \(x\), then \(z\) is part of \(u\), and \(\text{Cov}(x, u) \neq 0\). E.g., regressing wages on education while omitting ability (ability is in \(u\), and ability correlates with education). Reverse Causality (Simultaneity) If \(y\) also causes \(x\), then \(x\) and \(u\) are jointly determined — \(\text{Cov}(x, u) \neq 0\). E.g., regressing police per capita on crime rate, but crime may also cause police allocation. Measurement Error in x If \(x\) is measured with error (\(\tilde{x} = x + \text{error}\)), the measurement error is part of \(u\) and correlates with \(\tilde{x}\) — violating SLR.4. This causes attenuation bias (estimates biased toward zero).

docs.title: 3. Unbiasedness of OLS (Theorem 2.1)
docs.text:
Theorem: Under SLR.1–SLR.4:

\[E(\hat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0, \qquad E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\]

Proof for \(\hat{\beta}_1\):

Start from the OLS formula:

\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]

Substitute \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + u_i\) into the numerator. Using the fact that \(\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{x}) = 0\) (deviations sum to zero), the numerator simplifies to:

\[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(\beta_1 x_i + u_i) = \beta_1 \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) u_i\]

Therefore:

\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) u_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]

Taking the conditional expectation given \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}\) and applying SLR.4 (\(E(u_i \mid x_i) = 0\)):

\[E(\hat{\beta}_1 \mid x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \beta_1 + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) \cdot E(u_i \mid x_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2} = \beta_1 + 0 = \beta_1\]

By the law of iterated expectations, \(E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\). \(\blacksquare\)

The proof for \(\hat{\beta}_0\) follows similarly from \(\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\) and unbiasedness of \(\hat{\beta}_1\).

docs.title: 4. SLR.5 — Homoskedasticity
docs.text:
Assumption: The variance of \(u\) is constant across all values of \(x\):

\[\text{Var}(u \mid x) = \sigma^2\]

What this means: The spread of \(y\) around the conditional mean \(E(y \mid x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) is the same for all \(x\) — the error variance does not depend on \(x\).

Violation (Heteroskedasticity): If \(\text{Var}(u \mid x)\) varies with \(x\), the standard OLS standard errors are wrong (but OLS is still unbiased under SLR.1–SLR.4 alone). Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are the fix (covered in later modules).

docs.title: 5. Variance of OLS Estimators (Under SLR.1–SLR.5)
docs.text:
Theorem 2.2: Under SLR.1–SLR.5:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1 \mid x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_x}\] \[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_0 \mid x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \frac{\sigma^2 \cdot n^{-1} \sum x_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]

where \(SST_x = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2\).

Intuitions for \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)\):

Factor Effect on \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)\) Intuition Larger \(\sigma^2\) (noisier \(u\)) Increases variance More noise → harder to estimate the signal \(\beta_1\) Larger \(SST_x\) (more variation in \(x\)) Decreases variance More variation in \(x\) → better identification of slope Larger \(n\) Decreases variance (via \(SST_x \propto n\)) More data → more precise estimates

docs.title: 6. Estimating \(\sigma^2\): The Unbiased Estimator
docs.text:
Since \(\sigma^2 = E(u^2)\) (under \(E(u) = 0\)), a natural estimator is to average the squared residuals. However, the sample residuals \(\hat{u}_i\) are not the same as the true errors \(u_i\) — they satisfy two constraints (Properties 1 and 2 from M02.L03), which "use up" 2 degrees of freedom.

The unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is:

\[\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{SSR}{n - 2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i^2}{n - 2}\]

Why \(n - 2\)? We estimated 2 parameters (\(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\)), leaving \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom. It can be shown that \(E(\hat{\sigma}^2) = \sigma^2\) — \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\).

Using \(\hat{\sigma}^2\), the standard error of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is:

\[SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{SST_x}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}\]

where \(\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2}\) is called the standard error of the regression (also called the root MSE).

docs.title: 7. The Gauss-Markov Theorem (Preview)
docs.text:
Theorem (Gauss-Markov): Under SLR.1–SLR.5, the OLS estimators \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) are BLUE — Best Linear Unbiased Estimators.

  • Linear: \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is a linear function of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
  • Unbiased: \(E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) (from Theorem 2.1 above)
  • Best: \(\hat{\beta}_1\) has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators of \(\beta_1\)

What this means: If you insist on estimating \(\beta_1\) with a linear unbiased estimator, OLS is the most efficient choice — it extracts the maximum information from the data.

What this does NOT mean: If you allow biased estimators (e.g. ridge regression) or non-linear estimators, you might achieve lower mean squared error (MSE = bias² + variance) in finite samples. The Gauss-Markov theorem is about BLUE, not BUE (Best Unbiased Estimator).

The full proof of Gauss-Markov is in Wooldridge Appendix E (for the multiple regression case).

docs.title: Dataset: Education and Wages (continued from M02.L02)
docs.text:
Recall: \(n = 5\), \(\hat{\beta}_0 = -4.20\), \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 1.35\), \(SST_x = \sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 = 40\), \(SSR = 1.975\).

Step 1: Estimate \(\sigma^2\) and \(\hat{\sigma}\).

\[\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{SSR}{n-2} = \frac{1.975}{5-2} = \frac{1.975}{3} \approx 0.658\] \[\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{0.658} \approx 0.811\]

Interpretation: The typical residual (deviation from the fitted line) is about $0.81 per hour. Given that wages in this dataset range from $7.25 to $18.25, this is a small typical error — consistent with the high \(R^2 = 0.974\).

Step 2: Compute \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\).

\[SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{SST_x}} = \frac{0.811}{\sqrt{40}} = \frac{0.811}{6.325} \approx 0.128\]

Interpretation: The estimated standard deviation of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) across hypothetical repeated samples is about $0.13/hour per year. The estimated slope of $1.35 is about \(1.35 / 0.128 \approx 10.5\) standard errors away from zero — very strongly statistically significant (we'll formalise this in Module 4).

Step 3: Unbiasedness — conceptual illustration.

Suppose the true model is \(\text{Wage}_i = -3.00 + 1.20 \times \text{Educ}_i + u_i\) (i.e. \(\beta_0 = -3\), \(\beta_1 = 1.20\)). Under SLR.1–SLR.4, if we drew many random samples of size 5 and estimated OLS in each, the average of the resulting \(\hat{\beta}_1\) estimates would converge to \(1.20\). The single estimate from our data (\(\hat{\beta}_1 = 1.35\)) may deviate from \(1.20\) — unbiasedness is a property across all possible samples, not a guarantee for any individual sample.

This is why standard errors matter: they quantify how much we expect \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to vary from sample to sample.

Step 4: What violates SLR.4 here?

The regression \(\text{Wage} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Educ} + u\) violates SLR.4 if, for example, more-able workers both earn higher wages and tend to get more education. In that case, ability is in \(u\) and is correlated with \(\text{Educ}\), so \(E(u \mid \text{Educ}) \neq 0\). The OLS estimate of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) would then over-estimate the true causal effect of education, because it partially picks up the effect of ability. This is classic omitted variable bias — addressed in Module 3 (Multiple Regression).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Unbiasedness means my OLS estimate is close to the true β."

This is false. Unbiasedness is a property of the estimator across the distribution of possible samples, not a guarantee about any single estimate.

Formally: \(E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) means that if you repeatedly drew samples from the population and computed OLS, the average of your estimates would equal the true \(\beta_1\). Any single sample might give an estimate far from \(\beta_1\).

Analogy: A scale that is perfectly calibrated (unbiased — the average reading equals the true weight) can still give a very different reading each time you weigh the same object if the scale is very noisy. The precision of the scale is captured by its variance, not its unbiasedness.

In practice, we care about Mean Squared Error (MSE):

\[\text{MSE}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) + \underbrace{[\text{Bias}(\hat{\beta}_1)]^2}_{=\, 0 \text{ under SLR.1–SLR.4}}\]

Under SLR.1–SLR.4, OLS is unbiased, so \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)\). The Gauss-Markov theorem (SLR.1–SLR.5) then guarantees this variance is as small as possible among linear unbiased estimators. But a biased estimator with much lower variance might have lower MSE overall — this is the bias-variance tradeoff.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
For a sample of \(n = 30\) observations, you are given:

\[\sum_{i=1}^{30} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 120, \qquad SSR = 45\]

(a) Compute \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). (b) Compute \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\). (c) If \(n\) were doubled to 60 (with the same \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) and \(SST_x\) approximately doubling), what happens to \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\)?

Show Answer

(a) \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = SSR/(n-2) = 45/28 \approx 1.607\).

(b) \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = \hat{\sigma}/\sqrt{SST_x} = \sqrt{1.607}/\sqrt{120} = 1.268/10.954 \approx 0.1158\).

(c) With \(n = 60\), roughly \(SST_x \approx 240\) (doubling if \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) stays similar). \(\hat{\sigma}^2 \approx 45 \times 2/(58) \approx 1.552\) (SSR roughly doubles with double the observations). \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1) \approx \sqrt{1.552}/\sqrt{240} \approx 1.246/15.49 \approx 0.0804\). Approximately: \(SE\) scales as \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so doubling \(n\) reduces \(SE\) by a factor of \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\), from 0.116 to about 0.082. ✓

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
State whether each of the following violates SLR.4 (\(E(u|x) = 0\)), and if so, specify the likely direction of bias in \(\hat{\beta}_1\):

(a) Regressing salary on years of experience, omitting whether the person has a graduate degree (and graduate degrees are correlated with experience). (b) Regressing crop yield on rainfall, where rainfall is assigned by nature independently of soil quality. (c) Regressing a country's growth rate on its initial GDP, using data only on countries with GDP above $5,000 (sample selection). (d) Regressing hours worked on the reported wage rate, when workers misreport their wages by adding random noise (classical measurement error in \(x\)).

Show Answer

(a) Violates SLR.4. Graduate degree is in \(u\) (omitted), and it is likely correlated with experience (\(x\)) — people with graduate degrees may have more years of schooling and thus different experience profiles. If more experienced workers are more likely to have graduate degrees and graduate degrees increase salary, \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is positively biased (over-estimates the pure return to experience).

(b) Does NOT violate SLR.4 (likely). If rainfall is assigned by nature independently of soil quality (and other determinants of yield), then \(E(u \mid \text{rainfall}) = 0\) is plausible. This is analogous to a natural experiment — random assignment of the regressor satisfies the zero conditional mean assumption.

(c) Violates SLR.2 (random sampling) more than SLR.4 directly, but the effect propagates to bias. Restricting the sample to high-GDP countries introduces sample selection bias — the sample is not a random draw from all countries. OLS on this selected sample may be biased relative to the population relationship.

(d) Violates SLR.4. Classical measurement error in \(x\) causes attenuation bias: \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is biased toward zero (i.e. \(|E(\hat{\beta}_1)| < |\beta_1|\)). The measured \(\tilde{x} = x + e\) (where \(e\) is measurement noise) is correlated with the error in \(u\) (which contains \(-\beta_1 e\)), violating SLR.4.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
True or False — justify each:

(a) Under SLR.1–SLR.4, if we run OLS on 1000 different random samples and average all the \(\hat{\beta}_1\) estimates, we will get exactly \(\beta_1\). (b) If \(E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\), then \(\hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1\) in every sample. (c) Dividing SSR by \(n\) instead of \(n-2\) gives a biased estimator of \(\sigma^2\), and specifically it under-estimates \(\sigma^2\). (d) If SLR.5 (homoskedasticity) is violated, OLS is biased for \(\beta_1\).

Show Answer

(a) True in expectation (approximately true in practice). By the law of large numbers, the sample average of 1000 \(\hat{\beta}_1\) values converges to \(E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) as the number of replications grows. With 1000 replications, the average is very close to \(\beta_1\) but not exactly \(\beta_1\) due to sampling variation.

(b) False. Unbiasedness (\(E(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\)) is a statement about the expected value across samples. In any individual sample, \(\hat{\beta}_1\) will differ from \(\beta_1\) due to sampling error. Unbiasedness does not guarantee that any single estimate equals the true parameter.

(c) True. It can be shown that \(E\!\left[\frac{SSR}{n}\right] = \frac{n-2}{n}\sigma^2 < \sigma^2\). Dividing by \(n\) systematically under-estimates \(\sigma^2\). Dividing by \(n-2\) corrects for the 2 degrees of freedom consumed by estimating \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\), giving an unbiased estimate.

(d) False. OLS unbiasedness (Theorem 2.1) only requires SLR.1–SLR.4. SLR.5 (homoskedasticity) is not needed for unbiasedness. If SLR.5 is violated: OLS is still unbiased, but the formula \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2/SST_x\) is no longer correct, making standard errors and hypothesis tests invalid. The fix is to use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (covered in later modules).

docs.text:

  • Wooldridge: Appendix C, Section C.3 (Properties of estimators: unbiasedness, efficiency); this is the probability/statistics background assumed for Theorem 2.1
  • Omitted Variable Bias: Wooldridge Chapter 3 derives the OVB formula precisely for multiple regression — highly recommended follow-up
  • Gauss-Markov: Wooldridge Appendix E (formal proof); the simpler statement is in Chapter 2, Section 2.6
  • R: summary(lm(y ~ x))$sigma gives \(\hat{\sigma}\); vcov(fit) gives the variance-covariance matrix of \((\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1)\); coef(summary(fit))[, "Std. Error"] extracts standard errors
  • Python: results.bse gives standard errors; results.scale gives \(\hat{\sigma}^2\); np.sqrt(results.scale / np.sum((x - x.mean())**2)) manually computes \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\)
  • Simulation: A compelling way to understand unbiasedness is to simulate it in R/Python — generate data from a known DGP, run OLS 1000 times, and histogram \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to see it centred at \(\beta_1\)

docs.title: Lesson M03.L01: The Multiple Regression Model
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Specify and interpret a multiple regression model; explain why controlling for additional regressors produces ceteris paribus partial effects; recognise the link between simple-regression coefficient bias and omitted variables. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Sections 3.1–3.2)

docs.title: Why Multiple Regression?
docs.text:
Simple regression estimated the relationship between \(y\) and a single explanatory variable. That approach is rarely sufficient in economics because the world is multivariate. Any factor that

  1. affects \(y\), and
  2. correlates with the included regressor,

will distort the estimate if left out — a problem we formalise in M03.L04 as omitted variable bias (OVB).

Multiple regression solves this by including the relevant controls directly in the model, thereby isolating the partial or ceteris paribus effect of each regressor.

docs.title: The General Model
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\] Symbol Meaning \(y\) Dependent (outcome) variable \(x_1, \ldots, x_k\) Independent (explanatory) variables — the regressors \(\beta_0\) Intercept — value of \(y\) when all \(x_j = 0\) \(\beta_j\) (\(j \geq 1\)) Partial effect of \(x_j\) on \(y\), all else equal \(u\) Error term — everything that affects \(y\) but is not in the model

The model is called linear in parameters because each \(\beta_j\) enters linearly. The \(x_j\) themselves can be nonlinear transformations (logs, squares, interactions) — that is fine.

docs.title: Interpretation of \(\beta_j\): Ceteris Paribus
docs.text:
\[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x_j} = \beta_j \quad (\text{holding } x_1, \ldots, x_{j-1}, x_{j+1}, \ldots, x_k \text{ fixed})\]

Reading: A one-unit increase in \(x_j\) is associated with a \(\beta_j\)-unit change in \(y\), holding all other regressors constant.

This "holding constant" interpretation is the most important conceptual gain over simple regression. In the real world we cannot run controlled experiments for most economic questions, but multiple regression gives us the statistical equivalent of holding other factors fixed.

docs.title: Wage Equation Example
docs.text:
Consider estimating returns to education in the Australian labour market:

\[\text{wage} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \,\text{educ} + \beta_2 \,\text{exper} + \beta_3 \,\text{tenure} + u\]

where:

Variable Units Meaning wage AUD per hour Hourly wage educ years Years of formal education exper years Years of general work experience tenure years Years with current employer
  • \(\beta_1\) = return to one additional year of education, holding experience and tenure fixed
  • \(\beta_2\) = return to one additional year of experience, holding education and tenure fixed
  • \(\beta_3\) = return to one additional year of tenure, holding education and experience fixed

Without controlling for experience and tenure, a simple regression of wage on education would conflate the returns to education with the fact that more-educated workers tend to accumulate different experience profiles.

docs.title: How Adding Variables Changes Coefficients
docs.text:
Consider the simple regression:

\[\widetilde{\text{wage}} = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \tilde{\beta}_1 \,\text{educ}\]

versus the multiple regression above. In general \(\tilde{\beta}_1 \neq \hat{\beta}_1\) because:

  • exper and tenure both affect wage (\(\beta_2, \beta_3 \neq 0\))
  • exper and tenure correlate with educ

The simple-regression coefficient \(\tilde{\beta}_1\) picks up direct returns to education plus the indirect correlation through experience/tenure. The multiple regression coefficient \(\hat{\beta}_1\) isolates only the direct effect. The difference is OVB (formalised in M03.L04).

Key insight: The multiple regression coefficient on \(x_1\) is numerically equivalent to what you would get by (1) regressing \(x_1\) on all other regressors and taking the residuals \(\tilde{r}_1\), then (2) regressing \(y\) on \(\tilde{r}_1\) alone. This is the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem and makes the "partialling out" interpretation precise.

docs.title: When Adding Variables Hurts
docs.text:
A common misconception is that you should always add more regressors. This is wrong for two reasons:

  1. Inflated standard errors: Including irrelevant variables (variables with \(\beta_j = 0\)) does not reduce bias (there is nothing to remove) but does inflate the variances of all estimators — you lose efficiency. (Formalised in M03.L05.)

  2. Multicollinearity: Highly correlated regressors make it hard for OLS to tell their effects apart. Standard errors balloon, and coefficients become imprecise even if individually significant in the population.

  3. Overfitting: With too many regressors relative to sample size, in-sample fit rises spuriously while out-of-sample forecasts worsen.

The discipline of deciding which variables belong in the regression (i.e., have nonzero \(\beta_j\) and are not redundant) is specification analysis — a central econometric skill.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: A researcher estimates the following model using 526 Australian workers from the HILDA survey:

\[\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = 0.284 + 0.092\,\text{educ} + 0.041\,\text{exper} - 0.00071\,\text{exper}^2 + 0.022\,\text{tenure}\]

(a) Interpret \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.092\).

Because the dependent variable is \(\ln(\text{wage})\), a one-year increase in education is associated with approximately a \(0.092 \times 100 = 9.2\%\) increase in hourly wage, holding experience and tenure constant.

(b) Why is \(\text{exper}^2\) included?

Labour economists typically find that wage growth from experience is concave — each additional year adds less as the worker ages. Including \(\text{exper}^2\) allows for this diminishing return. The marginal effect of experience on \(\ln(\text{wage})\) is:

\[\frac{\partial \ln(\text{wage})}{\partial \text{exper}} = 0.041 - 2(0.00071)\,\text{exper} = 0.041 - 0.00142\,\text{exper}\]

At \(\text{exper} = 10\) years this equals \(0.041 - 0.0142 = 0.0268\), i.e., approximately 2.7% per year.

(c) Why does the intercept (0.284) have little economic meaning here?

\(\beta_0\) is the predicted \(\ln(\text{wage})\) when educ = exper = tenure = 0 — a worker with no education or work history. This is outside the support of the data and has no economic interpretation. Do not over-read intercepts in practice.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
Adding more variables always improves the regression

False. Adding an irrelevant variable (\(\beta_j = 0\) in the population) does not bias the remaining coefficients but inflates their standard errors, making hypothesis tests less powerful. The adjusted \(R^2\) (covered in M03.L02) can actually fall when an irrelevant regressor is added. Use economic theory and prior evidence to justify each variable's inclusion — do not kitchen-sink.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Model specification. A researcher wants to study the effect of class size on student test scores (NAPLAN) in Australian primary schools. List three variables you would add as controls. For each, explain (a) why it likely affects test scores and (b) why it might correlate with class size.

  2. Ceteris paribus. Suppose you estimate: $\(\widehat{\text{crime rate}} = 15.3 - 0.42\,\text{police officers} + 0.61\,\text{unemployment rate}\)$ A city council argues: "Cities with more police have higher crime rates, so hiring police causes crime." Critique this reasoning using the concept of ceteris paribus and explain what the regression actually tells us.

  3. Effect of adding a variable. You first estimate \(\tilde{\beta}_1 = 0.12\) (simple regression of log-wage on education). After adding experience and tenure you find \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.09\). What does this change suggest about the correlation between education and the omitted variables? Is the bias upward or downward in the simple regression?

docs.title: Lesson M03.L02: OLS Estimation in Multiple Regression
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Derive OLS estimators in multiple regression; interpret \(R^2\) and adjusted \(\bar{R}^2\); understand why \(R^2\) alone is insufficient for model selection. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Sections 3.2–3.3)

docs.title: OLS in Multiple Regression: The Objective
docs.text:
Given the model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\), OLS chooses estimates \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1, \ldots, \hat{\beta}_k\) to minimise the sum of squared residuals (SSR):

\[\min_{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots,\hat{\beta}_k} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_{i1} - \cdots - \hat{\beta}_k x_{ik}\bigr)^2\]

In simple regression (one regressor) the first-order conditions give explicit formulas. With \(k > 1\) regressors the FOCs are a system of \(k+1\) equations — solved most cleanly in matrix notation.

docs.title: Matrix Notation (Awareness Level)
docs.text:
Stack the data into matrices:

\[\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix}y_1\\\vdots\\y_n\end{pmatrix}_{n\times 1}, \quad \mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1k}\\\vdots & & & \vdots\\1 & x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{nk}\end{pmatrix}_{n\times(k+1)}, \quad \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\vdots\\\beta_k\end{pmatrix}_{(k+1)\times 1}\]

The OLS estimator in closed form is:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}\]

Requirements for this formula to exist:

  • \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})\) must be invertible — equivalent to MLR.3 (no perfect collinearity)
  • \(n > k + 1\) — more observations than parameters

You are not expected to derive this result from scratch in ECMT5001, but you should recognise the notation and understand that the scalar formulas for \(k=1\) are a special case.

docs.title: Fitted Values and Residuals
docs.text:
Once \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is obtained:

\[\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \hat{\beta}_k x_{ik}\] \[\hat{u}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]

These definitions are identical to simple regression — the OLS residual is always the actual minus fitted value.

docs.title: Algebraic Properties of OLS
docs.text:
These properties follow mechanically from the first-order conditions and hold for any OLS regression (simple or multiple):

Property Statement Zero mean residuals \(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i = 0\) Orthogonality \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}\hat{u}_i = 0\) for each \(j = 1,\ldots,k\) Sample means on surface \((\bar{x}_1, \ldots, \bar{x}_k, \bar{y})\) lies on the OLS regression surface SST decomposition \(SST = SSE + SSR\) where \(SSE = \sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\)

The orthogonality conditions say the residuals are uncorrelated with every included regressor in the sample. This is a mechanical property — it does not imply \(E(u|x_j) = 0\) in the population (that requires Assumption MLR.4).

docs.title: \(R^2\) in Multiple Regression
docs.text:
\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR}{SST} = \frac{SSE}{SST}\]

This is identical to the simple-regression formula. \(R^2\) is the fraction of the total variation in \(y\) explained by all regressors jointly.

Key mechanical fact: \(R^2\) never decreases when you add a regressor. Why? OLS can always set the new coefficient to zero and reproduce the old fit; any nonzero coefficient can only reduce SSR further.

This makes \(R^2\) a poor model-selection criterion — it will always favour the kitchen-sink model.

docs.title: Adjusted \(R^2\) (Penalised Fit)
docs.text:
To penalise for adding extra parameters, define:

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)} = 1 - \frac{n-1}{n-k-1}(1 - R^2)\] Component Meaning \(SSR/(n-k-1)\) Estimated residual variance \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) — penalises for each parameter used \(SST/(n-1)\) Sample variance of \(y\) — fixed

Properties of \(\bar{R}^2\):

  • Can be negative (when the regression fits worse than the intercept-only model)
  • Decreases when an added variable contributes less than its "fair share" to fit reduction
  • \(\bar{R}^2 \leq R^2\) always (equality when \(k=0\))
  • A regressor raises \(\bar{R}^2\) if and only if its \(|t\text{-stat}| > 1\) (approximately)
\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{s_y^2}\]

where \(s_y^2 = SST/(n-1)\) is the sample variance of \(y\). This framing makes clear: adding a regressor raises \(\bar{R}^2\) iff it reduces the estimated residual variance \(\hat{\sigma}^2\).

docs.title: Which to Report?
docs.text:
• \(R^2\): useful for describing how much variation is explained; always report it.
  • \(\bar{R}^2\): use for comparing models with different numbers of regressors on the same sample and same \(y\).
  • Neither is appropriate for comparing models with different transformations of \(y\) (e.g., \(\ln y\) vs \(y\)), because \(SST\) changes.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
A researcher estimates two models on \(n = 100\) observations of Australian workers:

Model 1: \(\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\,\text{educ}\)

Statistic Value \(SSR_1\) 48.6 \(SST\) 72.0 \(R^2\) 0.325 \(\bar{R}^2\) ?

Model 2: \(\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\,\text{educ} + \hat{\beta}_2\,\text{exper} + \hat{\beta}_3\,\text{tenure}\)

Statistic Value \(SSR_2\) 40.3 \(SST\) 72.0 \(R^2\) 0.440 \(\bar{R}^2\) ?

Step 1: Compute \(\bar{R}^2\) for Model 1 (\(k=1\), \(n=100\))

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{48.6/98}{72.0/99} = 1 - \frac{0.4959}{0.7273} = 1 - 0.682 = 0.318\]

Step 2: Compute \(\bar{R}^2\) for Model 2 (\(k=3\), \(n=100\))

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{40.3/96}{72.0/99} = 1 - \frac{0.4198}{0.7273} = 1 - 0.577 = 0.423\]

Step 3: Compare

Model \(k\) \(R^2\) \(\bar{R}^2\) 1 (educ only) 1 0.325 0.318 2 (educ + exper + tenure) 3 0.440 0.423

Both \(R^2\) and \(\bar{R}^2\) rise from Model 1 to Model 2, confirming that experience and tenure are jointly contributing meaningfully to explained variation — they are not just soaking up degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Compute \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) for Model 2

\[\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{SSR}{n-k-1} = \frac{40.3}{96} = 0.4198\]

This is the estimated variance of the error term \(u\), used in constructing standard errors for each \(\hat{\beta}_j\).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
\(R^2\) increasing when you add a variable means the variable belongs

False. \(R^2\) mechanically increases with every added regressor, even noise. A variable with a \(t\)-statistic of 0.1 will still raise \(R^2\). Always check (1) \(\bar{R}^2\) — did it rise? (2) the \(t\)-statistic — is the coefficient statistically different from zero? (3) economic theory — does the variable belong in the model on substantive grounds? All three should support inclusion.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Algebraic property. Prove that \(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i = 0\) in any OLS regression that includes an intercept. (Hint: The intercept column in \(\mathbf{X}\) is a column of ones; use the orthogonality condition \(\sum x_{i0}\hat{u}_i = 0\) where \(x_{i0} = 1\).)

  2. Adjusted \(R^2\) calculation. A researcher estimates a model with \(n = 50\), \(k = 5\), and reports \(R^2 = 0.72\). Calculate \(\bar{R}^2\). Then suppose they add 5 more irrelevant regressors and \(R^2\) rises to 0.76. Calculate the new \(\bar{R}^2\) and explain whether the additional regressors improved the model.

  3. Model comparison. Two models are estimated on the same \(n=200\) sample:

  4. Model A: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + u\); \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.41\)
  5. Model B: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4 + u\); \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.39\)

Which model do you prefer and why? What does it imply about \(x_2, x_3, x_4\)?

docs.title: Lesson M03.L03: Gauss–Markov Assumptions and BLUE
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: State and interpret the six MLR assumptions; articulate the Gauss–Markov theorem and what BLUE means; identify which assumption is most likely violated in applied work and what consequence follows. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Section 3.3), Chapter 3 Appendix

docs.title: The Six MLR Assumptions
docs.text: The properties of OLS — unbiasedness, efficiency, and valid inference — depend on which assumptions hold. Wooldridge labels these MLR.1–MLR.6.

docs.title: MLR.1 — Linear in Parameters
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\]

The model is linear in the \(\beta_j\)'s. The \(x_j\)'s can be nonlinear functions of underlying variables (e.g., \(\ln(\text{wage})\), \(\text{age}^2\), \(\text{educ} \times \text{female}\)) — as long as each enters the equation multiplied by a single \(\beta_j\).

Violation: A truly nonlinear parameter structure, e.g., \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1^{\beta_2} x\). Such models require nonlinear least squares (NLLS).

docs.title: MLR.2 — Random Sampling
docs.text:
The observed data \(\{(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik},y_i) : i=1,\ldots,n\}\) constitute a random sample from the population described by MLR.1.

Consequence of violation: Survey non-response bias, cluster sampling without correction, or time-series data (where observations are autocorrelated) can all violate MLR.2. Results still hold under weaker conditions (e.g., stationarity in time-series), but require more care.

docs.title: MLR.3 — No Perfect Collinearity
docs.text:
In the sample, no independent variable is an exact linear combination of the others. Equivalently, \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) has full rank \(k+1\).

Example violation: Including both "male" and "female" dummies (each 0/1) when those are the only two groups — they sum to 1, exactly equal to the intercept column. OLS cannot be computed.

Important: MLR.3 is about perfect collinearity only. High (imperfect) multicollinearity is permitted but inflates standard errors — see M03.L05.

docs.title: MLR.4 — Zero Conditional Mean (Exogeneity)
docs.text:
\[E(u \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k) = 0\]

The error term has zero mean conditional on all values of all included regressors. This is the most important assumption for unbiasedness of OLS.

It rules out: - Omitted variables that correlate with any \(x_j\) (M03.L04) - Simultaneity / reverse causality (e.g., wages affecting education choices) - Measurement error in regressors (M10)

When MLR.4 fails, OLS is biased and inconsistent — the gold-standard fix is instrumental variables (M10).

docs.title: MLR.5 — Homoskedasticity
docs.text:
\[\text{Var}(u \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k) = \sigma^2\]

The variance of the error is constant across all covariate values. Combined with MLR.4, this gives \(E(u^2 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma^2\).

Consequence of violation (heteroskedasticity): OLS remains unbiased (MLR.4 intact) but is no longer BLUE — a weighted least squares (WLS) estimator has smaller variance. The standard errors reported by default OLS are also incorrect; use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (M06).

docs.title: MLR.6 — Normality of the Error
docs.text:
\[u \mid x_1,\ldots,x_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

Implies MLR.4 and MLR.5. Needed for exact finite-sample \(t\)- and \(F\)-tests under OLS.

In large samples: By the Central Limit Theorem, \(t\)-statistics are asymptotically standard normal even without MLR.6, so this assumption becomes less critical as \(n\) grows. For small samples (e.g., \(n < 30\)), violation of normality can distort inference.

docs.title: The Gauss–Markov Theorem
docs.text:
Gauss–Markov Theorem

Under MLR.1–MLR.5, the OLS estimator \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is BLUE: Best Linear Unbiased Estimator.

Breaking down BLUE:

Letter Meaning B (Best) Among all linear unbiased estimators, OLS has the smallest variance for every \(\beta_j\) L (Linear) The estimator is a linear function of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) U (Unbiased) \(E(\hat{\beta}_j) = \beta_j\) for all \(j\) E (Estimator) It is a specific estimator, not a guess

"Best" in the BLUE sense means: for any other linear unbiased estimator \(\tilde{\beta}_j\),

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) \leq \text{Var}(\tilde{\beta}_j)\]

This is a minimum variance result — OLS squeezes the most information out of the data, given the constraints.

docs.title: Which Assumptions Drive What?
docs.text: Result Assumptions Required OLS is unbiased: \(E(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \boldsymbol{\beta}\) MLR.1–MLR.4 OLS is efficient (BLUE) MLR.1–MLR.5 OLS \(t\)-tests are exact in finite samples MLR.1–MLR.6 OLS \(t\)-tests are asymptotically valid MLR.1–MLR.4 + CLT (large \(n\))

docs.title: Worked Example: Economic Violations of Each Assumption
docs.text:
Context: A researcher estimates the effect of rainfall on crop yield for 200 Australian wheat farms:

\[\text{yield}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{rain}_i + \beta_2\,\text{fertiliser}_i + \beta_3\,\text{soil quality}_i + u_i\] Assumption Potential Violation Consequence MLR.1 True relationship is \(\text{yield} = \beta_0 \cdot \text{rain}^{\beta_1}\) (Cobb-Douglas) OLS fitted model is misspecified; must use NLLS or log-transform MLR.2 Farms selected because they're large (size-biased sample) Estimates may not generalise to all farms; selection bias MLR.3 Researcher includes both sand_fraction and clay_fraction where they sum to 1 (together with silt_fraction already included) OLS fails: singular matrix; drop one category MLR.4 Fertiliser use is chosen by the farmer partly in response to expected yield (reverse causality) OLS estimate of \(\beta_2\) is biased; need IV MLR.5 Variance of yield is much larger for farms with high rainfall (heteroskedasticity) OLS is unbiased but standard errors are wrong; use robust SEs MLR.6 Yield has a left-skewed distribution (bounded below at zero; catastrophic failures create a fat left tail) \(t\)-tests are approximate in small samples; large-sample CLT still applies

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
OLS is the best estimator (full stop)

The Gauss–Markov theorem says OLS is best among linear unbiased estimators — not among all possible estimators. If MLR.5 fails (heteroskedasticity), weighted least squares (WLS) is a linear estimator that is also unbiased and beats OLS on variance. If the error is known to be non-normal, some maximum likelihood estimators can dominate OLS in small samples. BLUE is not "best estimator ever" — it is "best in a specific class under specific conditions."

Multicollinearity violates MLR.3

Only perfect collinearity violates MLR.3. Imperfect multicollinearity (high \(R_j^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on other regressors) is perfectly consistent with MLR.3 — OLS remains BLUE. The problem with imperfect multicollinearity is large standard errors, not bias or breakdown of the estimator.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Assumption mapping. For each of the following scenarios, state which MLR assumption is violated and whether OLS is (a) biased, (b) inefficient, or (c) invalid for inference:
  2. (i) The error variance is three times larger for firms with revenues above $1 billion.
  3. (ii) A model of house prices omits suburb fixed effects, and suburb correlates with both price and included regressors (number of bedrooms, bathrooms).

  4. (iii) A researcher includes male (0/1) and female (0/1) as the only two gender dummies with a constant.

  5. BLUE theorem. An alternative linear estimator for \(\beta_1\) is the "split-sample estimator" \(\check{\beta}_1 = (\bar{y}_H - \bar{y}_L)/({\bar{x}_H - \bar{x}_L})\), where \(H\) and \(L\) denote the top and bottom halves of the \(x_1\) distribution. This estimator is linear in \(y\) and unbiased under MLR.1–MLR.4. What does the Gauss–Markov theorem imply about its variance relative to \(\hat{\beta}_1^{OLS}\)?

  6. MLR.4 vs MLR.5. Explain in one paragraph why MLR.4 (zero conditional mean) is more damaging to violate than MLR.5 (homoskedasticity). In what sense does heteroskedasticity "only" affect efficiency and standard errors, while endogeneity affects the coefficients themselves?

docs.title: Lesson M03.L04: Omitted Variable Bias
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Derive the omitted variable bias formula; determine the direction and magnitude of bias given the sign of the omitted variable's true coefficient and its correlation with the included regressor; apply OVB reasoning to real economic examples. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Section 3.3)

docs.title: What Is Omitted Variable Bias?
docs.text:
Omitted variable bias (OVB) arises when a variable that belongs in the true regression — because it affects \(y\) and correlates with at least one included regressor — is left out. The OLS estimate of the included regressor's coefficient absorbs part of the omitted variable's effect and is therefore biased.

OVB is a violation of MLR.4: the omitted variable ends up in the error term \(u\), making \(E(u \mid x_1) \neq 0\).

docs.title: The OVB Formula (Two-Variable Case)
docs.text:
True model (population):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u, \quad E(u \mid x_1, x_2) = 0\]

Estimated model (researcher omits \(x_2\)):

\[y = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \tilde{\beta}_1 x_1 + v, \quad v = \beta_2 x_2 + u\]

The simple-regression OLS estimator of \(\tilde{\beta}_1\) is:

\[\tilde{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)^2}\]

Taking expectations (using the true model):

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \tilde{\delta}_1\]

where \(\tilde{\delta}_1\) is the auxiliary regression coefficient — the slope from regressing \(x_2\) on \(x_1\):

\[\tilde{\delta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)(x_{i2} - \bar{x}_2)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)^2}\]

Key formula

\[\boxed{E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \underbrace{\beta_2 \cdot \tilde{\delta}_1}_{\text{OVB}}}\]

Bias \(= \beta_2 \cdot \tilde{\delta}_1\)

docs.title: Direction of Bias
docs.text:
The sign of OVB depends on the signs of \(\beta_2\) and \(\tilde{\delta}_1\):

\(\beta_2 > 0\) (omitted var ↑ \(y\)) \(\beta_2 < 0\) (omitted var ↓ \(y\)) \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\) (omitted corr. positively with \(x_1\)) → Upward bias \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\) → Downward bias \(\tilde{\delta}_1 < 0\) (omitted corr. negatively with \(x_1\)) → Downward bias \(\tilde{\delta}_1 < 0\) → Upward bias

Mnemonic: Same signs → upward bias; opposite signs → downward bias

Note: "upward bias" means \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1) > \beta_1\) (OLS overestimates the true effect).

docs.title: Classic Example: Ability Bias in Returns to Education
docs.text:
True model:

\[\ln(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{educ} + \beta_2\,\text{ability} + u\]
  • \(\beta_2 > 0\): more able workers earn higher wages (ability raises \(y\))
  • \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\): more able individuals tend to acquire more education (ability correlates positively with educ)

OVB:

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \underbrace{\beta_2}_{>0} \cdot \underbrace{\tilde{\delta}_1}_{>0} > \beta_1\]

Conclusion: Simple OLS of log-wage on education overestimates the true return to education. Part of what we attribute to schooling is really the wage premium for ability.

docs.title: Australian Example: Family Background and Returns to Education
docs.text:
In Australia, children from wealthier family backgrounds tend to: 1. Achieve higher educational attainment (educ ↑) 2. Earn higher wages due to networks, cultural capital, and inherited advantages (wage ↑)

If a researcher regresses \(\ln(\text{wage})\) on educ without controlling for family background (SES index):

  • \(\beta_2 > 0\) (SES raises wages)
  • \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\) (SES correlates positively with education)

→ Upward OVB on \(\hat{\beta}_1\). The estimated return to education is inflated.

This has direct policy implications: if we overestimate returns to education, we may over-invest in tertiary subsidies relative to other interventions.

docs.title: Worked Example: Calculate Direction and Magnitude
docs.text:
Setup: A researcher has data on 500 workers and estimates:

\[\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = 0.50 + 0.12\,\text{educ} \qquad (\text{simple regression})\]

An econometrician reveals that the true model is:

\[\ln(\text{wage}) = 0.20 + 0.08\,\text{educ} + 0.04\,\text{ability} + u\]

The auxiliary regression of ability on educ gives:

\[\widehat{\text{ability}} = -1.2 + 0.9\,\text{educ} \implies \tilde{\delta}_1 = 0.9\]

Step 1: Compute predicted OVB

\[\text{OVB} = \beta_2 \cdot \tilde{\delta}_1 = 0.04 \times 0.9 = 0.036\]

Step 2: Check against formula

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \text{OVB} = 0.08 + 0.036 = 0.116\]

This is close to the observed \(\tilde{\beta}_1 = 0.12\) (small discrepancy due to sampling variation). ✓

Step 3: Direction of bias

\(\beta_2 = 0.04 > 0\) and \(\tilde{\delta}_1 = 0.9 > 0\) → upward bias. The simple regression overestimates the return to education by roughly \(0.036\) log-wage units (≈ 3.6 percentage points).

Policy implication: A policy that raises education by 1 year would produce an approximately 8% wage increase (true \(\beta_1 = 0.08\)), not the 12% suggested by the biased estimate.

docs.title: OVB with Multiple Included Regressors
docs.text:
In the general case with multiple included regressors \(x_1, \ldots, x_k\) and omitted variable \(x_{k+1}\):

\[\text{OVB on }\hat{\beta}_j = \beta_{k+1} \cdot \tilde{\delta}_j\]

where \(\tilde{\delta}_j\) is the coefficient on \(x_j\) in the auxiliary regression of \(x_{k+1}\) on all included \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\). Every included coefficient is potentially biased if the omitted variable correlates with it.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
Adding more variables always eliminates OVB

Partially true, but dangerous. Adding the correct omitted variable eliminates OVB. However:

  1. The added variable may itself be endogenous — then you introduce a new form of bias. For example, adding job type to control for ability may be a bad control if job type is partly caused by education.

  2. Proxy variables (e.g., IQ test scores as a proxy for ability) reduce but do not eliminate OVB, because the proxy is an imperfect measure.

  3. Adding irrelevant variables does not reduce any bias but inflates variance and can induce new near-multicollinearity.

Zero correlation means no OVB

If the omitted variable is uncorrelated with \(x_1\) (\(\tilde{\delta}_1 = 0\)), then \(\text{OVB} = \beta_2 \cdot 0 = 0\) even if \(\beta_2 \neq 0\). A variable that affects \(y\) but is uncorrelated with included regressors goes into the error term without biasing any coefficient — it only increases residual variance (\(\hat{\sigma}^2\)) and hence standard errors.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. OVB direction. A researcher estimates the effect of the minimum wage (minwage) on employment (emp) without controlling for regional economic conditions (local_gdp). Suppose the true model is:

$\(\ln(\text{emp}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln(\text{minwage}) + \beta_2 \ln(\text{local\_gdp}) + u\)$

with \(\beta_2 > 0\). Australian states with higher local GDP tend to set higher minimum wages (\(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\)). Without controlling for local_gdp, is the OLS estimate of \(\beta_1\) (the employment elasticity of the minimum wage) biased upward or downward? What does this imply about published estimates of minimum wage effects that don't control for regional conditions?

  1. Derive OVB. Start from the true model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u\) and the formula \(\tilde{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum(x_{i1}-\bar{x}_1)(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum(x_{i1}-\bar{x}_1)^2}\). Substitute the true model for \(y_i\) and show that \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \beta_2\tilde{\delta}_1\).

  2. Numerical OVB. True model: \(y = 1 + 2x_1 + 3x_2 + u\). Auxiliary regression: \(x_2 = 0.5 + 0.4x_1 + \epsilon\). You estimate the misspecified model \(y = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \tilde{\beta}_1 x_1 + v\). (a) Compute \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1)\). (b) Is OLS upward or downward biased? (c) How much does OLS overstate/understate the effect of \(x_1\)?

docs.title: Lesson M03.L05: Multicollinearity and Variance of OLS
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Derive the variance formula for OLS in multiple regression; define the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF); distinguish perfect from imperfect multicollinearity; explain consequences for inference without confusing multicollinearity with bias. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Section 3.4)

docs.title: Variance of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) in Multiple Regression
docs.text:
Under MLR.1–MLR.5, the sampling variance of the OLS estimator for \(\beta_j\) is:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j \cdot (1 - R_j^2)}\]

where:

Symbol Definition \(\sigma^2\) Population error variance (\(\text{Var}(u \mid \mathbf{x})\)) \(SST_j\) \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2\) — total sample variation in \(x_j\) \(R_j^2\) \(R^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on all other regressors \(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1},x_{j+1},\ldots,x_k\)

The standard error (square root of estimated variance) is:

\[\widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{SST_j \cdot (1 - R_j^2)}}\]

where \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = SSR/(n-k-1)\).

docs.title: Three Ways to Get Small Variance
docs.text:
From the formula, \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) is small when:

  1. \(\sigma^2\) is small — the regression model fits well; not much unexplained variation in \(y\)
  2. \(SST_j\) is large — plenty of variation in \(x_j\) in the sample; more signal
  3. \(R_j^2\) is small — \(x_j\) is not well explained by the other regressors; no multicollinearity

The third factor is what makes multicollinearity costly.

docs.title: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
docs.text:
Define the Variance Inflation Factor for \(\hat{\beta}_j\):

\[VIF_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}\]

So:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j} \cdot VIF_j\]

The factor \(\sigma^2/SST_j\) is what the variance would be if \(x_j\) were orthogonal to all other regressors (\(R_j^2 = 0\), so \(VIF_j = 1\)). Multicollinearity inflates this baseline by the factor \(VIF_j \geq 1\).

Rule of thumb:

\(VIF_j\) Interpretation \(1\) No collinearity; baseline variance \(1\)–\(5\) Mild; generally acceptable \(5\)–\(10\) Moderate; monitor closely \(> 10\) Severe; consider remedies

Some textbooks use VIF \(> 10\) as the threshold; others use VIF \(> 5\). Judgement and context matter.

docs.title: Perfect Multicollinearity (MLR.3 Violated)
docs.text:
Perfect multicollinearity: \(R_j^2 = 1\) — one regressor is an exact linear combination of others.

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j \cdot (1 - 1)} = \frac{\sigma^2}{0} = \infty\]

OLS breaks down completely — the matrix \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) is singular and \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) does not exist. Software will drop one of the collinear columns or throw an error.

Common causes:

  • Dummy variable trap: Including \(d_{\text{male}}\) and \(d_{\text{female}}\) with an intercept (they sum to 1)
  • Exact definitional relationship: Including both total_tax and income_tax + GST + other_tax when the latter three sum exactly to the former
  • Redundant transformation: Including \(x\) and \(2x\) simultaneously

docs.title: Imperfect Multicollinearity
docs.text:
Imperfect multicollinearity: \(R_j^2\) close to (but not equal to) 1.

OLS is still computable, unbiased, and BLUE — MLR.3 is not violated. However:

  • \(VIF_j\) is large → \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) is large
  • Standard errors are large
  • \(t\)-statistics are small → it is hard to detect that \(\beta_j \neq 0\) even when it truly is (Type II error)
  • Coefficient estimates are sensitive to small changes in the sample (overfitting)

The core problem: with highly correlated regressors, the data contain insufficient independent information to precisely estimate the separate effects.

docs.title: Economic Causes of Multicollinearity
docs.text:
1. Aggregate macroeconomic variables: GDP, consumption, and investment all trend together — high pairwise correlations in time series.

  2. Overlapping demographic controls: Age, years of experience, and years since leaving school are all highly correlated life-stage variables.

  3. Physical characteristics: Height and weight are highly correlated for human subjects.

  4. Lagged variables: Including \(x_t\), \(x_{t-1}\), \(x_{t-2}\) in a time-series model creates near-perfect collinearity if \(x\) is a smooth series.

docs.title: Remedies for Multicollinearity
docs.text:
Remedy How Caution Collect more data Larger \(n\) reduces \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) directly Not always feasible; may not solve collinearity if correlation is structural Drop a variable Remove one collinear regressor Only valid if the dropped variable doesn't belong — otherwise introduces OVB Principal components Replace correlated \(x\)'s with uncorrelated linear combinations Components lose economic interpretability Ridge regression Add penalty \(\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2\) to SSR Introduces bias; requires choice of tuning parameter \(\lambda\)

Note: If the collinear variable belongs in the model (non-zero \(\beta_j\)), dropping it trades multicollinearity for OVB — often a worse problem. The preferred solution is more data.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: A researcher regresses log-housing prices on three regressors: \(x_1\) = floor area (m²), \(x_2\) = number of bedrooms, \(x_3\) = number of bathrooms. All are likely correlated.

Auxiliary regressions (to compute \(R_j^2\)):

\(j\) Regress \(x_j\) on others \(R_j^2\) \(VIF_j\) 1 (floor area) \(x_2, x_3\) 0.82 \(1/(1-0.82) = 5.56\) 2 (bedrooms) \(x_1, x_3\) 0.75 \(1/(1-0.75) = 4.00\) 3 (bathrooms) \(x_1, x_2\) 0.88 \(1/(1-0.88) = 8.33\)

Baseline variance (if \(R_j^2 = 0\)):

Suppose \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 0.04\) and \(SST_3 = 200\) (variation in bathrooms). Then:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)_{\text{baseline}} = \frac{0.04}{200} = 0.0002\] \[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3) = 0.0002 \times VIF_3 = 0.0002 \times 8.33 = 0.001666\] \[SE(\hat{\beta}_3) = \sqrt{0.001666} \approx 0.0408 \quad \text{vs baseline } \sqrt{0.0002} \approx 0.0141\]

The standard error for \(\hat{\beta}_3\) is 2.89 times larger than it would be with no multicollinearity (since \(\sqrt{VIF_3} = \sqrt{8.33} \approx 2.89\)). This makes the \(t\)-statistic for \(\beta_3\) roughly 2.89 times smaller — harder to achieve statistical significance even if bathrooms genuinely affect price.

Diagnosis: \(VIF_3 = 8.33\) is in the "moderate to severe" range. The researcher should check whether floor area and bathrooms are nearly perfectly collinear, possibly because large homes always have many bathrooms. Adding the number of floors or age of building as an alternative dimension of heterogeneity may help.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
Multicollinearity biases OLS estimates

False. Under MLR.1–MLR.4, OLS is unbiased regardless of multicollinearity (as long as MLR.3 holds, i.e., no perfect collinearity). High \(R_j^2\) inflates \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) and standard errors — affecting efficiency and inference — but does not bias \(E(\hat{\beta}_j)\). Confusing multicollinearity with OVB is one of the most common errors in applied econometrics.

Dropping a correlated variable fixes multicollinearity without cost

Dropping a variable reduces multicollinearity but only "fixes" the problem costlessly if the dropped variable has \(\beta_j = 0\) in the true model. If \(\beta_j \neq 0\), you have traded a precision problem (large SE) for a bias problem (OVB) — and bias is generally worse because it cannot be fixed by collecting more data.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. VIF calculation. You have three regressors: income (\(x_1\)), consumption (\(x_2\)), savings (\(x_3\)), where by definition \(\text{savings} = \text{income} - \text{consumption}\).
  2. (a) What is \(R_3^2\) from regressing savings on income and consumption?
  3. (b) What is \(VIF_3\)?
  4. (c) What does this imply for \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)\)?

  5. (d) How would you fix this problem?

  6. Variance formula. In a regression of test scores on class size (\(x_1\)) and school funding (\(x_2\)) with \(n = 200\) Australian schools: \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 100\), \(SST_1 = 400\), \(R_1^2 = 0.65\).

  7. (a) Calculate \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)\) and \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\).

  8. (b) If the sample grew to \(n = 800\) (quadrupling), roughly how would \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\) change? (Hint: \(SST_1\) scales approximately with \(n\).)

  9. Remedies trade-off. A researcher finds VIF = 12 for one regressor. List two remedies and, for each, state the condition under which it is valid without introducing new bias. Then explain which remedy is theoretically preferable if the researcher has access to a much larger dataset.
